extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of scientific method; philosophers of science; scientists interested in foundations of induction
extracted.subtask_description: Analysis and formalization of the notion of cause for the purposes of inductive logic: how to define causes, what counts as conditions, relation of agents/patients, dispositions, and the epistemic requirements for treating an antecedent as a cause.

rubrics_metrics.name: Law of Universal Causation
rubrics_metrics.description: The truth that every fact which has a beginning has a cause; the recognition that invariability of succession is found by observation to obtain between every fact in nature and some other fact which has preceded it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This law is co-extensive with the entire field of successive phenomena and is the fundamental pillar of inductive science: the undoubted assurance that there is a law to be found if we knew how to find it is the source from which the canons of Inductive Logic derive their validity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cause must be a physical (phenomenal) antecedent, not an ontological 'efficient' cause
rubrics_metrics.description: When speaking of causes for inductive logic one should mean causes that are themselves phenomena (physical causes), not metaphysical or 'efficient' causes beyond experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The notion of causation required is that which can be gained from experience; no appeal to mysterious, non-empirical ties or to the 'essences' of things is necessary or useful for the logic of induction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cause defined as the invariable antecedent of a consequent
rubrics_metrics.description: The cause of a phenomenon is the antecedent (or set of antecedents) with which the consequent is invariably connected: the antecedent which the consequent invariably follows.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For the purposes of inductive rules, we require not merely that an antecedent has always preceded a consequent in past experience, but that we have reason to believe, given the present constitution of things, that it always will so; this universality is necessary to treat an antecedent as a cause.

rubrics_metrics.name: The true cause is the whole sum of positive and negative conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: Philosophically the cause is the sum total of the conditions—positive and negative—whose concurrence invariably produces the consequent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Negative conditions can be summarized as the absence of preventing or counteracting causes; for convenience negative conditions are often left implicit, but a complete statement of cause must, in principle, introduce all relevant conditions (examples: poisoning combined with bodily constitution; ladder slip together with weight).

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not privilege the proximate antecedent or a single condition without justification
rubrics_metrics.description: It is common but philosophically incorrect to single out one antecedent as 'the cause' while treating others as mere conditions; often the proximate event is emphasized because it occurs immediately before the effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One should be cautious of naming the most conspicuous or last condition as the cause (e.g., eating a dish, being within sphere of attraction); accuracy demands recognition of all indispensable conditions unless they are legitimately implied or irrelevant to the present purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agent vs. patient distinction is largely verbal; all positive conditions are agents
rubrics_metrics.description: The ordinary distinction between something that acts (agent) and something acted upon (patient) is verbal: what we call patients often act as agents in producing the observed effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that objects or systems typically contribute actively to phenomena (e.g., the stone and the earth both are active in gravitation; organs of perception are agents in producing sensations); avoid explanatory fictions that falsely externalize activity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Causation includes production of dispositions/properties (states of preparation)
rubrics_metrics.description: A cause may not produce an immediate event but may confer on an object a property or capacity that makes it a cause of future effects (e.g., gunpowder prepared to explode; a wall painted white has the property of producing a white sensation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat such produced capacities as legitimate parts of causal explanation: the effect may be a state that renders an object capable of producing other effects when further conditions obtain. In enumerating conditions for an event, include both the present capacities and the immediate antecedents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require belief in invariability into the future, not mere past regularity
rubrics_metrics.description: To call an antecedent a cause we must believe not only that it has always been followed by the consequent in past experience, but that, as long as the present constitution of things endures, it always will be so.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This epistemic requirement avoids absurd reversals (e.g., night causing day) and distinguishes genuine causal laws from mere historical succession. The criterion is forward-looking invariability, not just repeated past concurrence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mutual confirmation and conflict resolution among inductions
rubrics_metrics.description: All inductions which can be connected by ratiocination are confirmatory of one another; inductions that deduce incompatible consequences serve as tests of each other and indicate that one must be revised or more guardedly expressed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When weaker inductions are shown to be corollaries of stronger, their certainty increases; conversely, if an induction conflicts with stronger ones, the weaker must give way unless the stronger have been overgeneralized. Use deductive relations among generalizations to strengthen or reject inductions (example: Torricellian experiment strengthening atmospheric weight).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of mathematical (number and space) laws: rigorous but insufficient alone
rubrics_metrics.description: Laws of number and space (geometry) possess rigorous universality and are the standard of certainty, but from laws of space and number alone one can deduce only further laws of space and number, not laws of succession.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To derive laws of succession (temporal order) you must combine mathematical premises with additional premises expressive of known uniformities of succession (e.g., combine geometrical truths with dynamical laws to deduce motion-area proportionality). Avoid attempts to demonstrate succession solely from spatial/numerical axioms.
